summary: Describes the link bundling construct in GMPLS signaling for cases where a link identifier plus label cannot unambiguously identify the resource used by a path. It updates the interface identification TLVs. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Several lanes can be grouped into one road, but sometimes you must say which lane. This memo explains how to bundle links and still point to the exact one.

questions: what is link bundling in mpls te
how is bandwidth advertised for a bundled link
subtitle: How to group several parallel links into one advertised link while still naming the exact one an LSP uses.

tldr.problem: In GMPLS signaling, a link identifier plus a label sometimes cannot pinpoint the resource an LSP uses, for example when a link is made of several fibers and a time slot only has meaning within one fiber.
tldr.mechanism: The link is split into component links, each identified uniquely on its node. The group is advertised as one bundled link to OSPF or IS-IS, while signaling names the component link and the label.
tldr.outcome: Bundling reduces the routing information flooded, at the cost of some detail. The RFC also deprecates two interface identification TLV types. It updates RFC 3471, RFC 3472 and RFC 3473.

facts.value: At least one component link is alive

facts.label: Maximum Bandwidth
facts.value: Not used; replaced by Maximum LSP Bandwidth

today: RFC 4201 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2005, and it updates RFC 3471, RFC 3472 and RFC 3473. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Links Get Bundled
sections.content:
A traffic engineering (TE) link is a logical construct that groups information about physical resources between label switching routers (LSRs), for path computation and GMPLS signaling. Often the pair of TE link identifier and label identifies the resource an LSP uses. Sometimes it does not. The RFC's example is a link between SONET/SDH cross-connects made of several fibers: the label is a TDM time slot that is significant only within a particular fiber, so signaling must name the link, the fiber and the time slot.

Link bundling handles this case. It also serves a second purpose: improving routing scalability by reducing what OSPF and IS-IS must carry, through aggregation. As with any aggregation, some information is lost, so the RFC restricts what may be aggregated.
sections.eli5: A road with several lanes shows up as one line on a map. That keeps the map simple, but a driver still needs to know which lane to use.

sections.title: Component Links and Bundled Links
sections.content:
The resources of the TE link are divided into disjoint subsets so that the partition is minimal and, within each subset, a label alone is enough to identify the resource. Each subset is a component link, and the whole TE link is a bundled link. Component link identifiers must be unique for a given node, so a <component link identifier, label> pair identifies the resource exactly.

Both ends must partition the resources consistently and understand each other's component link identifiers.
sections.eli5: Each lane gets its own number, and the numbers cannot repeat on the same road. The lane number plus the position in the lane tells you exactly where you are.

sections.title: Restrictions and Routing Rules
sections.content:
All component links in a bundle must have the same Link Type (point-to-point or multi-access), the same TE metric and the same resource classes at each end, and must begin and end on the same pair of LSRs. A Forwarding Adjacency may be a component link, so a bundle can mix point-to-point links and FAs. Multi-access links may be bundled only if the same routers connect to each and the Designated Router is the same on each.

Component link identifiers MUST be unique across both TE link and component link identifiers on a node. Component links and bundled links may each be numbered or unnumbered, independently.

A bundled link is alive when at least one component link is alive. Liveness can be determined by OSPF or IS-IS hellos, RSVP Hello, LMP hellos or layer 1 or layer 2 indications. Once alive, it is advertised as a TE link and flooded.
sections.eli5: Lanes only go in one bundle if they are alike and run between the same two places. The road counts as open as long as at least one lane works.

sections.title: Signaling a Component Link
sections.content:
Routing floods the bundled link but not its components, so an LSP's explicit route usually names the bundled link only. Choosing the component link is then a local matter between the two LSRs. Signaling must still identify both component link and label, and the sender of the Path or REQUEST message always chooses the component link, in each direction for a bidirectional LSP. Component link identifiers travel in RSVP or CR-LDP messages as described in section 8 of RFC 3473.

TLV types 1, 2 and 3 SHOULD indicate component links in IF_ID RSVP_HOP objects and IF_ID TLVs: type 1 for IPv4 numbered, type 2 for IPv6 numbered and type 3 for unnumbered identifiers. Types 4 and 5 SHOULD NOT be used, and if the type 5 TLV is used it MUST NOT be first.

A unidirectional LSP SHOULD use a single TLV. A bidirectional LSP uses one or two: the first is the downstream component link, the second the upstream one, and a single TLV means both directions. When the same label is valid across all component links, two TLVs SHOULD be used: the first names the TE link of the bundle and the second carries a bundle scope label, the special value 0xFFFFFFFF.

When an error occurs, received TLVs SHOULD be copied into the IF_ID ERROR_SPEC object (RSVP) or IF_ID Status TLV (CR-LDP), so the specific components are identified.
sections.eli5: The sender decides which lane to use and says so in the message. If the same spot works in every lane, a special all-lanes marker is used instead.

sections.title: TE Parameters and Bandwidth Accounting
sections.content:
The RFC defines each advertised parameter for a bundled link. Link Type, TE metric and resource classes are those of the component links. The OSPF Link ID is the neighbour's Router ID for point-to-point links. Maximum Reservable Bandwidth is the sum over component links, and so is Unreserved Bandwidth at each priority. Maximum Bandwidth is not used; Maximum LSP Bandwidth, the maximum over component links at a priority, replaces it.

Admission control is done per component link. An LSP with bandwidth b and setup priority p fits if at least one component link has maximum LSP bandwidth of at least b at priority p. If several fit, the implementation chooses. If a component link goes down, its unreserved bandwidth is set to zero and the bundle's values are recomputed. If all component links are down, the bundled link MUST NOT be advertised into OSPF or IS-IS.
sections.eli5: Add up the free space in all lanes for the total. But a big truck needs one lane with enough room, so the biggest single lane matters too.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it only defines ways of using procedures from other documents, so it raises no new security issues for RSVP-TE or CR-LDP; any issues are covered in the referenced documents.

For IANA, the document changes the recommended usage of two Interface_ID types in the GMPLS Signaling Parameters registry. Type 4 (COMPONENT_IF_DOWNSTREAM) and type 5 (COMPONENT_IF_UPSTREAM) are now marked DEPRECATED.
sections.eli5: This memo only reuses safety rules that already exist elsewhere. Two old label types are crossed out of the official list.
